summary: Defines Session Description Protocol offer/answer procedures for negotiating and establishing a DTLS association, and the criteria for when a new one must be set up. It updates RFC 5763 and RFC 7345 by replacing their SDP-related text. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: SDP endpoints use tls-id values to identify a DTLS association. The value pair tells them whether a negotiation keeps the existing association or starts a new one.

subtitle: The tls-id attribute signals whether endpoints reuse or replace a secure association.

tldr.problem: An SDP offer or answer did not clearly indicate whether a new DTLS association was needed, especially when ICE changed its username fragment.
tldr.mechanism: The media-level tls-id value from each endpoint identifies an association; a new value signals that a new association should be established.
tldr.outcome: The RFC standardizes common DTLS offer/answer procedures, updates RFCs 5763 and 7345, and also describes use with TLS. RFC 9725 later updated it.

today: RFC 8842 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It updates RFC 5763 and RFC 7345, and has itself been updated by RFC 9725.

sections.title: A Shared Rule for DTLS Negotiation
sections.content:
RFC 5763 and RFC 7345 define SDP offer/answer procedures for particular DTLS uses. RFC 8842 provides common procedures so different usages can negotiate DTLS in the same way.

With ICE, a changed username fragment can mean ICE is newly negotiated or restarted. Those events do not always require a new DTLS association, and earlier SDP procedures did not let an endpoint explicitly signal that need. The new tls-id attribute addresses this gap.
sections.plainLanguage: Different applications need consistent SDP steps for setting up DTLS. The tls-id attribute gives endpoints a clear way to identify an association and request a new one.

sections.title: When an Association Must Change
sections.content:
After a successful offer/answer exchange, endpoints establish a new DTLS association if the negotiated setup roles change, a certificate fingerprint is added, removed, or changed, or an endpoint changes its tls-id value.

A new association can be established only through a successful offer/answer exchange. When a new association is needed, an endpoint MUST initiate that exchange and generate a new local tls-id value.
sections.plainLanguage: Changed roles, changed fingerprints, or a new tls-id value signal that endpoints need a new association. They agree on that change through SDP offer and answer.

sections.title: The tls-id Attribute
sections.content:
tls-id is a media-level SDP attribute. Its value contains 20 to 255 characters selected from letters, digits, plus, slash, hyphen, and underscore. The pair of values from the offerer and answerer identifies the association.

The value MUST come from a strong random function and include at least 120 bits of randomness. If the value and fingerprints stay unchanged, the endpoint indicates that it intends to reuse the existing association.
sections.plainLanguage: Each endpoint supplies its own random tls-id value. Together, the two values identify which DTLS association the endpoints are using.

sections.title: Offer and Answer Steps
sections.content:
An initial offer includes setup:actpass, one or more certificate fingerprints, and a unique tls-id. The offerer must be ready to receive a DTLS ClientHello before the answer arrives.

The answer includes its setup role and fingerprints. If a new association is required, the answerer supplies a new tls-id. If it accepts reuse, it repeats the previous value and fingerprints. The endpoints must verify that the certificate in the DTLS handshake matches a fingerprint from SDP.
sections.plainLanguage: The offer names the association and provides certificate fingerprints. The answer either confirms reuse or supplies a new identifier for a new association.

sections.title: ICE and Unordered Transports
sections.content:
ICE connectivity checks happen before the DTLS handshake. Over an unordered transport such as UDP, old and new DTLS packets could arrive together, so at least one endpoint MUST use a new transport/source-address/source-port combination for a new association.

The answerer cannot initiate a new DTLS association over such a transport unless the offerer started an ICE restart. An ICE restart by itself does not require a new DTLS association.
sections.plainLanguage: On UDP, old and new packets can arrive out of order. A new association therefore needs a new local transport address or port, or a new set of ICE candidates.

sections.title: TLS Use and Security
sections.content:
The same procedures can identify a TLS connection. When the SDP connection attribute says new, tls-id must be new; when it says existing, an existing tls-id value must be reused. The two attributes must not conflict.

The RFC says it does not change DTLS or SDP security properties. The TLS handshake certificate must match an SDP fingerprint, and endpoints must terminate the media session if it does not.
sections.plainLanguage: The tls-id rules also apply to TLS connections alongside the connection attribute. The document clarifies negotiation but does not change how DTLS security works.
